newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - U.S. inflation data to hold sway.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - U.S. inflation data to hold sway.

text.p: Inflation indicators will be the flavour of this week with U.S. data providing the main focus for financial markets, analysts said on Friday.
Elsewhere, confirmation of signs of a strengthening British economy are expected while towards the end of the week Germany will also be looking for inflationary signals.

"The market has become accustomed to weak (U.S.) inflation data but one of these days we're going to get a strong number and that will cause quite a lot of havoc," said Ian Gunner, international economist at Chase in London.
"We don't expect it to be this month but that's the point, when it does happen, nobody will expect it," he said.
September consumer prices due on Wednesday will be the main data to watch for having had some indication of inflation from Friday's producer prices.

Those figures showed a rise of 0.2 percent, slightly under the forecast of a 0.3 percent rise. With the U.S. markets closed on Monday for Columbus day, investors will have plenty of time to digest these figures, analysts said.

Analysts also noted the Philadelphia Fed Index was due on Thursday, the first leading indicator for October, along with September capacity utilisation and industrial production and August business inventories, while on Friday international trade data for August will be released.
"That may take the shine off the dollar," said Julian Jessop, chief European economist at Nikko Europe in London.
Analysts said there was a large trade deficit for July and if that were to be sustained in August there would be concerns about the dollar, particularly against the yen.
"There is a feeling the narrowing of the Japanese surpluses is starting to stall a little. That could raise some doubts about the dollar rally if the deficit stays wide," said Gunner.
In Europe, British employment data and PSBR for September and August average earnings will be published on Wednesday.

"As long as the data remains reasonably subdued then we could continue to see gilt yields chasing other yields lower but pieces of data like (average earnings) could cause problems if they come out on the strong side," said Gunner. "We could see an increasing amount of volatility in the gilt market."

Paul Mortimer-Lee, chief economist at Paribas Capital Markets in London, said people would be looking for any room for tax cuts from the PSBR data, while M4 on Friday should continue to tell the story of strong monetary growth and a strengthening economy.
In Germany September wholesale prices will be the data to watch, analysts said.

"At the moment the market is happy that inflation is going to remain low, but they might have a few second thoughts after these figures," said Mortimer-Lee. "You've got upside risk to these numbers both from strong commodity price rises and also from the weaker mark."
Also of interest, the possiblity of Italy's re-entry to the ERM, is to be discussed at a meeting of Italian and Finnish finance ministers on Monday.
Italian producer and wholesale price data is due on Thursday and analysts said it should be encouraging.
"What will be of concern is that the underlying environment remains favourable for a move to three percent in consumer price inflation," said Jessop.
Italian wholesale prices have already met that target showing an annualised rise of 2.6 percent in July, while July producer prices showed an anualised rise of 3.4 percent.
